content: The guidelines developed by WHO, in collaboration with UN-Habitat and various non-governmental organizations, will be made accessible on the WHO website. Additionally, an executive summary and outreach materials tailored for professionals in the health, housing, and urban planning sectors, as well as policymakers and program managers, will be created and distributed through WHO country offices and their partners. Technical support for adapting and implementing the Housing and Health Guidelines (HHGL) in specific countries will be provided upon request by ministries of health or WHO regional and country offices. Monitoring and evaluation are critical to assessing the impact of these guidelines. Health improvements can only be achieved if safer and healthier housing materials, practices, and principles are widely adopted, and if housing is properly maintained and replaced when necessary. Active monitoring will help determine the extent and locations of HHGL implementation, offering insights into progress and their health impacts. Member States are encouraged to consider establishing a housing quality surveillance system, similar to public health systems, to track these changes. One method to evaluate the HHGL's impact is by applying the environmental burden of disease approach to the healthy housing field. A methodological guide from the WHO European Region (2011) provides a framework for quantifying health effects from housing risks, which could be expanded globally to include additional risk factors covered by the HHGL. The implementation toolkit will include guidance on integrating monitoring and evaluation activities into existing data collection processes to minimize the burden on statistical offices and reporting bodies. WHO and its partners aim to secure funding to address interventions not reviewed in the HHGL, prioritize research questions to fill identified gaps, and determine effective methods for studying these questions. This includes areas such as access to green spaces, walking and cycling infrastructure, housing interventions to prevent vector-borne diseases, and ventilation improvements. Recommendations will also address multifactorial interventions and the relationship between health and other housing aspects, such as tenure security, residential mobility, structural integrity, and accessibility to public transport and community resources. WHO's housing definition encompasses not only the physical structure but also the immediate environment, including streets, recreational facilities, food sources, parks, and natural amenities. These environmental factors significantly influence health, highlighting the importance of urban and land-use planning as public health determinants. Further evidence-based guidance is needed to address these areas. Recommendations may also explore the connections between health and housing conditions, such as humidity, structural safety, and neighborhood walkability. Through the HHGL, WHO has the potential to support Member States in reducing health inequities by promoting healthier housing and urban conditions, contributing to global poverty reduction efforts. Guidance will be developed in collaboration with housing, planning, and settlement development sectors, as well as residents and non-governmental organizations, to prioritize actions in slums and informal settlements. This guidance will address key health threats in these areas, provide best practices for health promotion and prevention, and offer advice on implementing the HHGL and related interventions.
